**SCOP 1.75** (frozen 2009-02-23, released 2009-06-05) treated PDB 1acc chain A as a single domain:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| sid / sunid | d1acca_ / 43828 |
| sccs | f.11.1.1 |
| region | 1acc A: (entire chain) |

Its lineage was class f (membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides) -> fold f.11 "Anthrax protective antigen" (sunid 56987) -> superfamily f.11.1 (56988) -> family f.11.1.1 (56989) -> protein "Anthrax protective antigen" (56990) -> species Bacillus anthracis, TaxId 1392 (56991). That fold, superfamily and family each had exactly one child, and the species node held only whole-chain domains from 1acc, 1t6b and 1tzo. The classification was a one-protein branch built on one chain.

**Current SCOPe 2.08** (released 2021-09-22, latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16) splits the same chain into two domains in two different classes:

| sid | sunid | region | sccs |
|---|---|---|---|
| d1acca2 | 238522 | A:14-225 | b.179.1.1 |
| d1acca1 | 238521 | A:226-735 | f.60.1.1 |

The N-terminal domain sits in class b (all beta proteins) -> fold b.179 "Anthrax protective antigen N-terminal-like" (254104) -> superfamily b.179.1 "PA14-like" (254123) -> family b.179.1.1 "PA14" (254147) -> protein "PA14" (254334) -> species Bacillus anthracis (254763). The C-terminal domain stays in class f -> fold f.60 "Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like" (254103) -> superfamily f.60.1 (254122) -> family f.60.1.1 (254146) -> protein "Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like" (254333) -> species B. anthracis TaxId 1392 (254762).

**When:** release 2.03 (old label 1.75C, released 2013-10-09) still carried the single d1acca_ / f.11.1.1 domain, as did 2.01. Release 2.04 (released 2014-07-11) already shows the two-domain definition, and 2.05, 2.06, 2.07 and 2.08 are identical to it. So the split landed in 2.04. The old identifiers were retired rather than remapped: a request for sunid 43828 in 2.08 returns 404 "node was not found in the requested release", and sccs f.11 no longer resolves in 2.08. Note also that SCOPe selected a different PDB file revision for 1acc in the two releases (revision 1998-02-11 under 1.75 versus 2009-02-24 under 2.08), so the residue numbering underlying the 14-225 / 226-735 boundaries comes from the newer coordinate file.

## Why it matters for domains as evolutionary modules

The decisive new information was not a better look at this one protein. It was the discovery of the same N-terminal module elsewhere. Superfamily b.179.1 "PA14-like" in 2.08 holds four families: b.179.1.1 "PA14", b.179.1.2 "GLEYA domain", b.179.1.3 "Glycoside hydrolase family 31 (GH31), PA14-like domain" (sunid 418815) and b.179.1.0 "automated matches". Family b.179.1.1 itself contains two proteins, the B. anthracis PA14 module and a "Beta-glucosidase PA14 domain" protein (254417) represented by Kluyveromyces marxianus domains d3abza3, d3abzb3, d3abzc3, d3abzd3 and the 3ac0 chains at residues 388-559. Family b.179.1.2 contains Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces pastorianus adhesin-type domains; b.179.1.0 contains automatically classified members from B. anthracis, Komagataella pastoris and Pichia pastoris.

Three lessons follow.

1. **The evolutionary unit is the module, not the chain.** A single chain can carry two segments with independent histories. Here they are so structurally dissimilar that SCOPe places them in different classes, b and f. Any chain-level label averages unrelated signals and is wrong for at least one part of the chain.
2. **Domain boundaries are revisable hypotheses.** The 1.75 definition was not a curation error given the evidence of its time; it became untenable once homologs of one segment appeared in bacteria, yeasts and glycoside hydrolases. Modules recur in unrelated contexts, which is exactly what makes them modules.
3. **A singleton branch signals absent evidence, not absent homology.** The C-terminal part remains a one-family, one-protein superfamily in 2.08. That is a statement about what has been detected, not proof the segment is unique.

Keep the levels distinct. Shared membership in superfamily b.179.1 is a claim of common ancestry with low sequence identity, so the PA14 module of 1acc and the Kluyveromyces beta-glucosidase module are homologous. Shared membership in family b.179.1.1 is a stronger claim of clear sequence or functional relatedness. Fold level (b.179 versus f.60) and class level (b versus f) are structural bins and carry no homology claim at all. The two 1acc domains being in different classes says nothing about their relationship to each other beyond that they do not resemble each other structurally.

## How this should affect homology searches

- **Search with domain-level libraries at a pinned release.** Use the 2.08 boundaries A:14-225 and A:226-735, not a 1.75 whole-chain profile. A full-chain profile dilutes the PA14 signal and will produce alignments that run across the module boundary.
- **Report per-domain coverage.** A query matching only the N-terminal module should never be described as homologous to the whole chain, and vice versa. Require that alignment extent be reported against each domain separately, and reject hits whose coverage straddles the 225/226 junction without support on both sides.
- **Do not transfer function across the PA14 superfamily.** Hits linking the N-terminal module to yeast adhesin GLEYA domains or to GH31 glycoside hydrolase modules are superfamily-level homology. PA14-type modules occur in proteins with entirely different activities, so a PA14 match licenses a statement about module ancestry only. Inferring the host protein's biochemical role from a PA14 hit is unsound in both directions, and the fold/class relationship f.60 versus b.179 licenses nothing.
- **Treat the "automated matches" family as weaker evidence.** Family b.179.1.0 members were placed by automated methods rather than manual curation, so they should not be used to anchor a curated homology claim or to seed a benchmark positive set without independent checking.
- **Audit pipelines keyed to old identifiers.** Anything storing d1acca_ or sunid 43828, or using ASTRAL sequences derived from 1.75, is silently working with obsolete whole-chain boundaries, and 43828 does not resolve in 2.08. Re-map through PDB code plus residue range, not through sunid, and record the release version with every result.
- **Watch representative selection.** Under 1.75 this structure contributes one whole-chain representative; under 2.08 it contributes two, in different classes. Mixing releases in one library or benchmark creates both boundary errors and inconsistent class labels. Pick one release and state it.
- **External evidence needed to confirm any such split or hit.** Profile-profile or hidden Markov model comparison such as HHsearch against Pfam, where the PA14 module corresponds to PF07691; structural superposition and structure-comparison scores from DALI or FATCAT, and SCOPe's own structure-hit and sequence-hit services for the chain; SIFTS and UniProt domain annotation to verify boundaries in homologous sequences that lack structures. Functional claims require experimental assay data, which no classification database supplies.

## Limits on this answer

SCOPe 2.08 is not comprehensive (is_comprehensive is false), so absence of a relative in f.60.1 is absence of curated evidence, not evidence of absence. The split date is bracketed to between the 2.03 and 2.04 freezes by the per-release domain listings; the API responses I used give domain definitions and lineage, not curator rationale, so the reason for the split is inferred from the module's cross-kingdom distribution visible in b.179.1, not read from a changelog.
